title: Resurrection, not transmigration
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ τὸν περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως λόγον (πολὺν ὄντα καὶ δυσερμήνευτον καὶ δεόμενον σοφοῦ εἴπερ τι ἄλλο τῶν δογμάτων καὶ ἐπὶ πλεῖον διαβεβηκότος, ἵνα τὸ ἄξιον τοῦ θεοῦ παραστήσῃ καὶ τὸ μεγαλοφυὲς τοῦ δόγματος, διδάσκοντος λόγον ἔχειν σπέρματος τὸ καλούμενον κατὰ τὰς γραφὰς σκῆνος τῖς ψυχῆς, ἐν ᾧ „οἱ“ δίκαιοι „ὄντες“ στενάζουσι „βαρούμενοι,“ μὴ θέλοντες αὐτὸ „ἐκδύσασθαι ἀλλ᾿ ἐπενδύσασθαι“) μὴ νοήσας ὁ Κέλσος τῷ ἀπὸ ἰδιωτῶν καὶ μηδενὶ λόγῳ παραστῆσαι δυναμένων ἀκηκοέναι περὶ αὐτοῦ χλευάζει τὸ λεγόμενον, χρήσιμον πρὸς τοῖς ἀνωτέρω εἰρημένοις ἡμῖν περὶ τούτου τοῦτο μόνον ὑποσημειώσασθαι πρὸς τὸν λόγον, ὅτι οὐχ, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος, τῆς μετενσωματώσεως παρακούσαντες τὰ περὶ ἀναστάσεώς φαμεν ἀλλ᾿ εἰδότες ὅτι ἡ τῇ ἑαυτῆς φύσει ἀσώματος καὶ ἀόρατος ψυχὴ ἐν παντὶ σωματικῷ τόπῳ τυγχάνουσα δέεται σώματος οἰκείου τῇ φύσει τῷ τόπῳ ἐκείνῳ· ὅπερ ὅπου μὲν φορεῖ ἀπεκδυσαμένη (τὸ) πρότερον ἀναγκαῖον μὲν περισσὸν δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὰ δεύτερα. ὅπου δὲ ἐπενδυσαμένη ᾧ πρότερον εἶχε, δεομένη κρείττονος ἐνδύματος εἰς τοὺς καθαρωτέρους καὶ αἰθερίους καὶ οὐρανίους τόπους. καὶ ἀπεξεδύσατο μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν τῇδε γένεσιν ἐρχομένη τὸ χρήσιμον πρὸς τὴν ἐν τῇ ὑστέρᾳ τῆς κυούσης, ἕως ἦν ἐν αὐτῇ, χορίον· ἐνεδύσατο δὲ ὑπ᾿ ἐκεῖνο ὃ ἦν ἀναγκαῖον τῷ ἐπὶ γῆς μέλλοντι διαζῆν. εἶτα πάλιν ὄντος τινὸς „σκήνους“ ἐπιγείου οἰκίας, ἀναγκαίας που τῷ σκήνει, καὶ καταλύεσθαι μέν φασιν οἱ λόγοι τὴν ἐπίγειον οἰκίαν „τοῦ σκήνους“ τὸ δὲ σκῆνος ἐπενδύσασθαι „οἰκίαν ἀχειροποίητον αἰώνιον ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς.“ λέγουσι δὲ οἱ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι „τὸ“ μὲν „φθαρτὸν ἐνδύσασθαι αὐτὸ ἀφθαρσίαν,“ τὴν διαφέρουσαν τοῦ ἀφθάρτον, „τὸ“ δὲ „θνητὸν ἐνδύσασθαι ἀθανασίαν,“ ἕτερον τυγχάνον τοῦ ἀθανάτου. ὃν γὰρ λόγον ἔχει σοφία πρὸς τὸ σοφὸν καὶ δικαιοσύνη πρὸς τὸ δίκαιον καὶ εἰρήνη πρὸς τὸ εἰρηνικὸν, τοῦτον τὸν λόγον ἀφθαρσία μὲν πρὸς ἄφθαρτον ἀθανασία δὲ πρὸς ἀθάνατον. ὅρα οὖν ἐφ᾿ οἷα προτρέπει ὁ λόγος, „ἐνδύσασθαι“ λέγων τὴν „ἀφθαρσίαν“ καὶ τὴν „ἀθανασίαν,“ ἅτινα ὡς ἐνδύματα τῷ ἐνδυσαμένῳ καὶ περιεχομένῳ τῶν τοιούτων ἐνδυμάτων οὐκ ἐᾷ φθαρῆναι ἢ ἀποθανεῖν τὸν περικείμενον αὐτά. καὶ ταῦτα δ᾿ ἡμῖν ἀποτετολμήσθω διὰ τὸν μὴ νοήσαντα ὅ τι ποτὲ λέγομεν τὴν ἀνάστασιν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο γελῶντα καὶ χλευάζοντα ὃν οὐκ οἶδε λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: Since the doctrine (λόγος) about the resurrection (ἀνάστασις) (being much, hard to interpret (δυσερμήνευτος), and needing a wise man (σοφός) if any other of the doctrines (δόγματα), and one advanced (διαβαίνω) further, so that he may present what is worthy (ἄξιον) of God and the greatness of nature (μεγαλοφυές) of the doctrine, teaching (διδάσκοντος, taken with δόγματος) that what is called according to the scriptures the tent (σκῆνος) of the soul has the principle (λόγος) of a seed (σπέρμα), in which the righteous, being, groan (στενάζω) being burdened (βαρέομαι), not wishing to put it off (ἐκδύομαι) but to put on over (ἐπενδύομαι)), Celsus not having understood (νοέω), by having heard about it from laymen (ἰδιῶται) unable to present it by any reasoning, mocks (χλευάζω) what is said, it is useful, besides what we said above about this, to note (ὑποσημειόομαι) only this toward his argument: that not, as Celsus thinks, having misheard (παρακούω) transmigration (μετενσωμάτωσις) do we speak of resurrection, but knowing that the soul, by its own nature incorporeal (ἀσώματος) and invisible (ἀόρατος), being in any bodily place (τόπος σωματικός), needs a body proper (οἰκεῖον) to the nature of that place; which it wears (φορέω), sometimes having stripped off (ἀπεκδύομαι) the former, necessary but superfluous (περισσόν) relative to the second things, sometimes having put on over what it had before, needing a better garment (ἔνδυμα) for the purer, ethereal (αἰθέριοι) and heavenly (οὐράνιοι) places. And it stripped off, coming to birth (γένεσις) here, what was useful for life in the womb (ὑστέρα) of the one pregnant (κυέω), while it was in it, the chorion (χορίον, fetal membrane); and put on beneath that what was necessary for one about to live (διαζάω) on earth. Then again, there being a certain ‘tent’, an earthly house (ἐπίγειος οἰκία) somehow necessary to the tent, the words (λόγοι) say the earthly house ‘of the tent’ is dissolved (καταλύω) but the tent puts on over ‘a house not made with hands (ἀχειροποίητος), eternal (αἰώνιος) in the heavens’. And the men of God say ‘the perishable (φθαρτόν)’ puts on (ἐνδύομαι) ‘imperishability (ἀφθαρσία)’, differing from the imperishable (ἄφθαρτον), and ‘the mortal (θνητόν)’ puts on ‘immortality (ἀθανασία)’, being other than the immortal (ἀθάνατον). For what relation (λόγος) wisdom (σοφία) has to the wise, righteousness to the righteous, peace to the peaceful, this relation imperishability to imperishable, immortality to immortal. See then to what the word urges (προτρέπω), saying ‘put on’ imperishability and immortality, which as garments to the one who put on and is enclosed (περιέχομαι) by such garments do not allow the one wearing (περίκειμαι) them to perish or die. And let these things have been ventured (ἀποτολμάω) by us because of the one not understanding what we mean by the resurrection and therefore laughing (γελάω) and mocking a doctrine which he does not know.
pass_b_english: The doctrine of the resurrection is large and hard to explain. If any doctrine needs a wise man, and one far advanced, it needs one to set forth what is worthy of God and the grandeur of the doctrine, which teaches that what the Scriptures call the tent of the soul has the character of a seed: the tent in which the righteous groan, being burdened, not wishing to put it off but to put on over it (2 Corinthians 5:4). Celsus did not understand this doctrine; because he heard about it from unlearned people who could not set it forth with any reasoning, he mocks what is said. So, in addition to what we said about it earlier, it is useful to note only this in reply to his argument: we do not speak of resurrection, as Celsus thinks, because we have misheard the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

We speak of it because we know that the soul, which in its own nature is bodiless and invisible, when it is in any bodily place, needs a body suited to the nature of that place. This body it wears, at times having stripped off what was necessary before but is superfluous for its second state, and at times having put it on over what it had before, since it needs a better garment for the purer, ethereal, and heavenly places. So, when it came to birth here, it put off the membrane that was useful for its life in the womb of the mother who carried it, while it was there; and beneath that it had put on what was necessary for one who was to live on earth.

Then again, since there is a “tent” with an earthly house that is in some way necessary to the tent, the Scriptures say that the earthly house “of the tent” is dissolved, but that the tent puts on over itself “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1). And the men of God say that “the perishable” puts on “imperishability,” which differs from the imperishable, and that “the mortal” puts on “immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53), which is something other than the immortal. For as wisdom is related to the wise, and righteousness to the righteous, and peace to the peaceful, so imperishability is related to the imperishable, and immortality to the immortal. See, then, to what the passage urges us, when it speaks of putting on imperishability and immortality. Like garments on one who has put them on and is wrapped in them, these do not allow the one who wears them to perish or die.
We have ventured even this much because of the man who did not understand what we mean by the resurrection, and for that reason laughs and mocks at a doctrine he does not know.

choices.choice: The opening Greek is one long sentence with a parenthesis describing the doctrine; it is broken into several English sentences without dropping any clause, and the main clause (‘it is useful to note’) is kept as the conclusion with ‘So’. διδάσκοντος is taken with the adjacent δόγματος (‘the doctrine, which teaches’); it can also agree with the wise man (‘a wise man … teaching that’), with no change to the doctrine stated. ‘Has the character of a seed’ (λόγον ἔχειν σπέρματος) likely alludes to 1 Corinthians 15:36–38 (the sown seed and the body given to it); possible allusion, not cited inline. ‘Groan, being burdened, not wishing to put it off but to put on over it’ is 2 Corinthians 5:4 (5:2 also has ‘groan’ and ‘put on over’); the object of ἐπενδύσασθαι is unstated, so no ‘another’ is supplied. ὄντος τινὸς σκήνους ἐπιγείου οἰκίας is compressed; rendered ‘a “tent” with an earthly house’, following 2 Corinthians 5:1 ‘the earthly house of the tent’. οἱ λόγοι in ‘the Scriptures say’ means the sacred words of 2 Corinthians 5:1; ‘the men of God’ refers to the apostolic writer of 1 Corinthians 15:53. ὁ λόγος in ‘see to what the passage urges’ is the scriptural saying. χορίον is the outer fetal membrane; rendered ‘membrane’. ‘Transmigration of souls’ answers Celsus’s charge, reported indirectly here (Christians misheard the doctrine of reincarnation), so it carries no quotation marks. ‘What we said about it earlier’ points to Origen’s earlier treatment of the resurrection in this work. Koetschau’s supplement (τό) before πρότερον and the misprint τῖς for τῆς and ἀφθάρτον for ἀφθάρτου in the staged text do not affect the sense.
Dangling ‘teaching that …’ fixed to ‘the doctrine, which teaches that …’ (διδάσκοντος with δόγματος); alternative noted
Removed added ‘another’ in ‘put on another over it’ (2 Corinthians 5:4 states no object)
Restored the Greek logic: the English had made ‘Since’ govern ‘he mocks’; now Celsus’s failure is stated, and the main clause ‘it is useful to note’ follows with ‘So’
‘there is a “tent” and an earthly house’ (added ‘and’) to ‘a “tent” with an earthly house’
‘because of a man who’ to ‘because of the man who’ (τὸν μὴ νοήσαντα, i.e. Celsus)
2 Corinthians 5:1, 5:4 and 1 Corinthians 15:53 checked against the Greek wording
